reasoning: Set B has the stronger RL design and fits the user's constraints more closely. It uses random plus scripted baselines everywhere, value and policy ladders (tabular → DQN rungs, REINFORCE → PPO), reward shaping, partial observability, co-learning rungs with controls and a version tournament, all on free CPU tooling in one sensible package. But its build plan is stale against its own architecture. AD-16/AD-17 redesigned the core around sides and schedules, the contract retired `registry.make_agent` for `make_agents`, and PL-01 gained `run_streams`, `make_schedule` and the colearn steps. M1's plan was never replanned: M1-T01 and M1-T03 still Read the retired `registry.make_agent`, so their packets failed to generate ('dt context failed'). That means the very first ready task, the interface, cannot be handed to a builder. No M1 task builds `run_streams`, `make_schedule` or the solo schedule that `train_loop` and the entry sketch need. M1-T09 still names `<learner>/<reward>/seed-<n>` folders. The architecture also keeps process narration ('On approval: pipeline-design updates…', 'M1 is at 0 of 20 tasks'). Set A strays further from the ground truth. It has no random baseline. It adds a rented-GPU budget (QR-02 $5) against the free-tools constraint. It adds a library-twin goal that spawns a probe-gated M4. Its tank design admits fish see the ball only one step before contact, so they can't dodge it. It is over-split into 12 packages. Still, its M1 is internally consistent: the plan, contract, packets, todo and dependency graph agree, every packet I sampled is complete, and the walking skeleton can start building now. Executability decides it for A.
